title: HIVE: Harnessing Human Feedback for Instructional Visual Editing
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving instructional image editing so that generated edits better match human intentions and preferences. The authors argue that existing instruction-based editing systems can misinterpret instructions, over-edit images, or produce results that do not align well with what users want. To address this, they propose HIVE (Harnessing Human Feedback for Instructional Visual Editing), a framework that adds human preference learning to diffusion-based image editing.

HIVE is a three-stage approach. First, the authors perform instructional supervised fine-tuning using a large dataset of image-instruction-edit triplets, including newly collected training data and data derived from InstructPix2Pix. Second, they collect human rankings of multiple edited outputs for the same image-instruction pair and train a reward model to predict human preference. Third, they fine-tune the diffusion model using the learned rewards, either by weighting examples according to reward or by conditioning on reward labels.

The study uses synthetic evaluation data and a self-collected 1,000-example user-study dataset of real images and human-written instructions, with crowdsourced annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk. The results show that incorporating human feedback improves alignment with instructions and preserves irrelevant parts of images better than the baseline model trained without feedback. The authors also report that the reward-conditioning variant performs slightly better in stability, and that cycle-consistency augmentation improves performance.

The paper concludes that human feedback is valuable for instruction-following image editing, but it also notes several limitations and risks: some instructions are still hard to understand, counting and spatial reasoning remain failure cases, object grounding can be wrong, and the model may inherit bias or harmful content from foundation models. The authors also mention that cases where all candidate outputs are similarly wrong are not helped much by preference learning, and that some edited outputs can become unstructured.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical generative-model paper, not an education study, and it does not evaluate student or teacher outcomes, school settings, or instructional practice. The paper reports model-training procedures, benchmark comparisons, and user preference studies for image editing quality, but no educational intervention evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no demonstrated impact on education outcomes or teacher coaching. Any gains are within the domain of image-editing model preference and alignment, so the education-relevant impact is not assessable from this paper.

interventions.use_case: human-feedback-guided diffusion model fine-tuning for instructional visual editing (image editing from text instructions)
